name: Inverse Square Law and Calculations
what: This subtopic covers Newton's law of universal gravitation, the inverse square law for gravitational field strength, and how to calculate gravitational field strength and gravitational force using g = GM/r² and Fg = Gm₁m₂/r².
why: These formulas are the quantitative tools for analysing gravitational interactions at any scale — from objects on Earth's surface to satellites in orbit and planets around the Sun. They appear in almost every gravitational fields exam question.

items.title: I can state and explain the inverse square law for gravitational fields
items.what: The gravitational field strength g is inversely proportional to the square of the distance r from the mass: g ∝ 1/r². Doubling the distance reduces the field strength to one-quarter; tripling the distance reduces it to one-ninth.
items.why: The inverse square law explains why gravity weakens with distance and allows field strength at any location to be calculated or compared without needing to know the mass of the body if a reference value is known.
items.example: At Earth's surface (r = RE), g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹. At two Earth radii from the centre (r = 2RE), g = 9.81/4 = 2.45 N kg⁻¹. At three Earth radii (r = 3RE), g = 9.81/9 = 1.09 N kg⁻¹.

items.title: I can calculate gravitational field strength using g = GM/r²
items.what: The gravitational field strength at a distance r from a mass M is given by g = GM/r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The variable r is measured from the centre of mass of the body, not from its surface.
items.why: This formula allows calculation of the gravitational field strength at any point around any mass, including at the surface of planets, moons, and at orbital altitudes.
items.example: To find g at the International Space Station (408 km above Earth's surface): r = (6.37 × 10⁶) + (4.08 × 10⁵) = 6.778 × 10⁶ m. Then g = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴) / (6.778 × 10⁶)² = 8.67 N kg⁻¹.

items.title: I can use the inverse square law ratio method to find field strength at a new distance
items.what: When the surface gravitational field strength of a body is known but its mass is not, the field strength at a new distance can be found using the ratio: g₂/g₁ = (r₁/r₂)². The mass M cancels and is not needed.
items.why: This method is efficient in exam situations where the mass of a body is not provided but the surface gravity and radii are given, such as when finding the field strength at a satellite's orbital altitude.
items.example: Mars has a surface gravity of 3.72 N kg⁻¹ and radius 3390 km. A satellite orbits at 3690 km from the centre. g_orbit = 3.72 × (3390/3690)² = 3.14 N kg⁻¹.

items.title: I can state Newton's law of universal gravitation and identify what each symbol represents
items.what: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses m₁ and m₂ separated by distance r is Fg = Gm₁m₂/r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The distance r is measured between the centres of mass of the two objects.
items.why: This law is the foundation of all gravitational force calculations and explains how gravity operates between any two masses in the universe, from apples and Earth to planets and the Sun.
items.example: Two physics students, each of mass 60 kg, sit 1.0 m apart. The gravitational force between them is F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 60) / (1.0²) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁷ N — far too small to detect without sensitive instruments.

items.title: I can calculate the gravitational force acting on a mass using Fg = mg
items.what: In a known gravitational field of strength g, the gravitational force on a mass m is Fg = mg. This is equivalent to Newton's second law (F = ma) when gravity is the only force, since the acceleration equals the field strength.
items.why: This formula links the gravitational field concept (g in N kg⁻¹) to the force acting on any mass placed in that field, and directly gives the weight of an object at any location.
items.example: An astronaut of mass 80 kg standing on the Moon (g = 1.61 N kg⁻¹) experiences a gravitational force of Fg = 80 × 1.61 = 129 N, compared to 784 N on Earth's surface.

items.title: I can apply Newton's third law to gravitational forces between two masses
items.what: The gravitational force that mass A exerts on mass B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force that mass B exerts on mass A. Both forces are always attractive and act along the line joining the centres of mass.
items.why: Newton's third law applied to gravity explains why both objects in a gravitational interaction accelerate toward each other, though the more massive object accelerates far less noticeably.
items.example: Earth exerts a gravitational force of approximately 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. By Newton's third law, the Moon exerts an equal force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on Earth — this force causes Earth's tides.
